title: Finite-Time Singularity Formation for the Three-Dimensional Euler Equations
summary: [This is a guest post by Matei P. Coiculescu . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] The Euler equations model the motion of an inviscid fluid: fluid motion in the absence of shear stresses arising from fluid particles “sliding past” each other. In an ideal fluid the dynamics are time-reversible since the arrow of time in a real, viscous fluid is determined by the loss of kinetic energy due to the internal friction of the fluid. We also make the distinction of working with the incompressible Euler equations, where the fluid density is assumed to be constant throughout the fluid. Even with all of these assumptions away from the true behavior of fluid motion, the incompressible Euler equations remain useful in modeling, for instance, the amount of lift generated by an airfoil. We can also choose to work with a fluid that occupies a so-called “periodic box”, or a cube with the sides identified. Henceforth we will let this box be with opposite faces identified. This is an assumption often used in numerical simulations of the Euler equations, where it is easier to consider periodic boundary conditions in space rather than deal with the behavior of the fluid at infinity (computers don’t seem to like infinity). We also assume that the fluid is a continuum rather than a collection of particles, to allow for analysis to be performed.
